newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi dissident bin Laden seen as serious threat.
newsitem.headline: Saudi dissident bin Laden seen as serious threat.

text.p: Saudi dissident Osama bin Laden has the ammunition to execute his latest threats of holy war against the United States and its allies -- charisma, die-hard followers and the cash to fund violence, analysts said on Tuesday.

In an interview from his headquarters in Afghanistan for a British television programme broadcast last week, bin Laden said the United States was occupying and violating Islam's greatest and holiest lands and must be expelled.
Bin Laden said bombings in Riyadh in 1995 and al-Khobar last June that killed 24 Americans were a warning to Washington.

"The bombings...were a clear indication for the crusading forces to correct this grave mistake and for them to depart before it is too late and before the battle begins in earnest," he said in an interview filmed by one of his followers.
Bin Laden, who has previously spent time in Sudan and Yemen, denied involvement in the blasts targeting the tight alliance between Washington and Riyadh.
The U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia told Americans in the kingdom on Tuesday that "planning for terrorist action against U.S. interests in Saudi Arabia continues unabated".
Its latest security warning also expressed concern over the bin Laden interview.

Analysts and Saudi opposition figures said it was hard to estimate how many followers bin Laden has across the Middle East and Afghanistan, where he commanded a force of so-called "Arab Afghans" against Soviet occupying troops in the 1980s.
But they agreed that whatever the number, bin Laden has the firepower, ideological credentials and network of zealots to execute and inspire holy war against American targets.
"I think one has to take these threats seriously," said Phillip Robbins, a Middle East expert at Oxford University.
"Based on his past activities one should take seriously the threat of possible bombings or assassinations."

The big question, analysts and Saudi opposition figures say, is what kind of damage bin Laden can do in Saudi Arabia, a strategic ally of the United States and the world's largest oil producer and exporter.
Three of the four Saudis who were beheaded for the Riyadh blast fought in Afghanistan.
Saad al-Fagih, London-based leader of the Movement for Islamic Reform in Arabia, said bin Laden's followers in the kingdom were Saudi "Arab Afghans".
But he added that bin Laden's influence reaches beyond his die-hard followers.

"He is the godfather of all people who believe in force. People who belong to other groups are motivated by his speeches and actions," said al-Fagih. "Because of his charisma, he is a symbol of jihad (holy war)."
One expert estimated bin Laden has about 500 hard-core followers in Saudi Arabia.
The U.S. State Department recently called bin Laden "one of the most significant sponsors of Islamic extremist activities in the world today".
Bin Laden, who called for a holy war against the United States last year, is a financier of hard-line groups seeking to bring down governments from Egypt to Algeria.
He lives in Afghanistan under the protection of the Taleban radical Islamic student militia who seized control of the Afghan capital Kabul last year.
The rebel leader, son of a Saudi construction magnate, was stripped of his Saudi citizenship in 1994. He is reckoned by some Middle East sources to command a fortune of $300 million.

Although he lives abroad, bin Laden still makes the Saudi authorities nervous. He is a sensitive topic in the kingdom and most media coverage of his activities consists of condemnation by clerics, Saudi analysts say.
"In the old days, before he was an outlaw, Osama was popular with all kinds of people here. He was from a rich family and this opened doors. Now it's not clear how many followers he has," said one.
"The Saudi government wants him to go away and be quiet."
